subject: Pathology
vignette: A 58-year-old woman with obesity, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and hypertriglyceridemia undergoes ultrasound for right upper quadrant pain and is found to have a bright, diffusely echogenic liver. Liver biopsy shows hepatocytes distended by large clear cytoplasmic vacuoles that displace the nucleus to the periphery. There is no significant fibrosis and no inflammation.
question: Which of the following best explains this intracellular accumulation?

options.text: Accumulation of lipofuscin pigment from lipid peroxidation
Deposition of hemosiderin after recurrent hemorrhage
Fatty change with cytoplasmic accumulation of lipid vacuoles
Beta-pleated sheet protein deposits forming amyloid
Deposition of bilirubin due to biliary obstruction

explanation_correct: Steatosis, or fatty change, is the accumulation of lipid within parenchymal cells, and in the liver it occurs with obesity, diabetes, and alcohol use. One mechanism is cell injury that decreases apolipoprotein synthesis, so triglycerides cannot be exported and accumulate as cytoplasmic vacuoles that displace the nucleus. This patient's metabolic risk factors and the clear vacuoles without fibrosis are the classic picture of uncomplicated steatosis, which is potentially reversible if the underlying cause is corrected.

explanation_incorrect.A: Lipofuscin is a yellow-brown wear-and-tear pigment composed of lipid and phospholipid polymers complexed with protein, associated with normal aging and derived from lipid peroxidation of membrane lipids; it does not form large clear vacuoles.
explanation_incorrect.B: Hemosiderin is an iron storage pigment that accumulates after hemorrhage or in iron overload and appears as golden-brown granular material rather than clear vacuoles.
explanation_incorrect.C: Amyloid is deposited extracellularly as an amorphous pink beta-pleated sheet protein, whereas the lipid here is intracellular.
explanation_incorrect.E: Bilirubin accumulation, as in obstructive jaundice, produces green-brown pigment within hepatocytes and bile canaliculi, not the clear fat vacuoles described.

educationalObjective: Steatosis is the intracellular accumulation of lipid, classically in the liver with obesity, diabetes, and alcohol use, partly because reduced apolipoprotein synthesis impairs triglyceride export.

subject: Pathology
vignette: A 78-year-old man dies of an unrelated illness, and at autopsy the pathologist notes fine yellow-brown pigment granules in hepatocytes and cardiac myocytes. The deposits are composed of polymers of lipids and phospholipids complexed with protein. The pathologist explains to a student that this pigment relates to cumulative oxidative damage over the patient's life. A separate finding in the same patient is an unrecognized old granulomatous lesion in the apex of the lung that is now densely mineralized.
question: Which of the following best describes these two findings, respectively?

options.text: Lipofuscin from lipid peroxidation, and dystrophic calcification of diseased tissue
Hemosiderin from hemorrhage, and metastatic calcification of normal tissue
Melanin from melanocytes, and psammoma body formation
Bilirubin from hemolysis, and fat necrosis with saponification
Amyloid from immunoglobulins, and caseous necrosis without mineralization

explanation_correct: Lipofuscin is a yellow-brown wear-and-tear pigment associated with normal aging, composed of lipid and phospholipid polymers complexed with protein and possibly derived from lipid peroxidation of polyunsaturated membrane lipids; autopsy of an older adult reveals deposits in the heart, colon, liver, kidney, and eye. The mineralized old lung lesion is an example of dystrophic calcification, which occurs in abnormal, diseased tissues such as old granulomatous infections like tuberculosis. Dystrophic calcification is localized and follows injury or necrosis.

explanation_incorrect.A: Hemosiderin is an iron pigment from hemorrhage or iron overload, and metastatic calcification deposits calcium in normal tissues, usually kidney, lung, and gastric mucosa, because of hypercalcemia or hyperphosphatemia.
explanation_incorrect.B: Melanin is a brown-black pigment of melanocytes and is not the aging pigment described, and psammoma bodies are concentrically laminated calcified spherules of specific tumors rather than old granulomas.
explanation_incorrect.C: Bilirubin accumulation produces jaundice from heme breakdown, and fat necrosis is lipase-mediated saponification of adipose tissue, which is unrelated to a mineralized apical lung lesion.
explanation_incorrect.D: Amyloid is beta-pleated sheet protein, not a lipid-protein wear-and-tear pigment, and old caseous lesions characteristically do undergo calcification as dystrophic calcification.

educationalObjective: Lipofuscin is a lipid-peroxidation derived wear-and-tear pigment of aging, and dystrophic calcification is calcium deposition in abnormal, previously diseased tissue such as old granulomas.

subject: Pathology
vignette: A 61-year-old woman with end-stage renal disease on dialysis is found to have serum calcium and phosphate values that are both elevated. Imaging shows diffuse bilateral nephrocalcinosis and an increased A-a gradient with interstitial infiltrates in the lung. She also reports excessive thirst and large volumes of dilute urine.
question: Which of the following best describes this patient's calcification?

options.text: Dystrophic calcification localized to an area of prior necrosis
Metastatic calcification of normal tissues from hyperphosphatemia
Psammoma bodies within a papillary carcinoma of the thyroid

explanation_correct: Metastatic calcification is deposition of calcium in normal tissues, is widespread rather than localized, and results from hyperphosphatemia such as in chronic kidney disease or from hypercalcemia as in primary hyperparathyroidism, sarcoidosis, or hypervitaminosis D. The deposits occur predominantly in the interstitium of the kidney, lung, and gastric mucosa, tissues that lose acid quickly so that an increased pH favors calcium deposition. Nephrocalcinosis of the collecting ducts can then cause nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, explaining this patient's polyuria and thirst, as well as renal failure.

explanation_incorrect.B: Dystrophic calcification occurs in abnormal, diseased tissue such as old tuberculous lesions, infarcts, or atherosclerotic plaques, is localized, and is secondary to injury or necrosis rather than to abnormal calcium and phosphate levels.
explanation_incorrect.C: Psammoma bodies are concentrically laminated calcified spherules seen in tumors such as papillary carcinoma of the thyroid and kidney, somatostatinoma, meningioma, mesothelioma, and ovarian serous papillary cystadenocarcinoma; they are not the diffuse visceral calcification of renal failure.
explanation_incorrect.D: Amyloid is an extracellular beta-pleated sheet protein that binds Congo red and shows apple-green birefringence, distinct from basophilic calcium deposits on H&E staining.
explanation_incorrect.E: Fat necrosis with chalky-white saponification results from lipase action in acute pancreatitis or breast trauma and is localized to adipose tissue, unlike this diffuse process.

educationalObjective: Metastatic calcification deposits calcium in normal tissues due to hyperphosphatemia or hypercalcemia, favors kidney, lung, and gastric mucosa, and can cause nephrocalcinosis with nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.
